## August 24, 1931 — A Monday Shared With History

Some dates accumulate. August 24 has appeared at enough consequential moments that arriving on it places you in a specific line — not of coincidence exactly, but of the calendar's recurring use of the same address.

---

**Eighteen hundred and fifty-two years before your birth, Vesuvius erupted.** The traditional date of the eruption that buried Pompeii is August 24, 79 AD — established through two letters the Roman writer Pliny the Younger sent to the historian Tacitus, describing what he witnessed from across the bay as a teenager. The column of ash rose twelve miles. Pompeii was buried under fifteen to twenty feet of volcanic debris in under twenty-four hours. The city was preserved so completely that when it was excavated beginning in the eighteenth century, it offered a frozen cross-section of Roman daily life — bread still in ovens, graffiti still on walls, bodies in the postures of their final moments. You arrived on the date that, for nearly two thousand years, has marked one of the most complete destructions and strangest preservations in Western history.

**A hundred and seventeen years before your birth, the British burned Washington.** On August 24, 1814, during the War of 1812, British troops marched into the American capital, met almost no resistance, and set fire to the White House, the Capitol, the Treasury, and other public buildings. President Madison had already fled. Dolley Madison famously remained long enough to save a portrait of George Washington before the flames reached the mansion. It remains the only occasion since the British departed in 1783 that a foreign military force has occupied and burned the capital of the United States. One hundred and seventeen years later, on the same date, you were born in a country whose capital had never again been touched.

**Fifty-four days before you arrived, two men flew around the world in less than nine days.** On July 1, 1931, Wiley Post and Harold Gatty landed in New York, completing the first around-the-world flight in history — 15,474 miles in 8 days, 15 hours, and 51 minutes, with twelve stops across Alaska, Russia, Germany, England, Canada, and back. When they landed, they were given a ticker-tape parade. You were born into a world where this was still recent news, where aviation was understood as the most transformational technology of the era, and where a transatlantic crossing still meant a week on an ocean liner for anyone who wasn't a record-seeking aviator. In your lifetime, that transatlantic journey became a seven-hour routine.

**A democratic republic had just replaced a monarchy in Spain, and the ground was already shifting.** On April 14, 1931, municipal elections in Spain showed such overwhelming republican sentiment that King Alfonso XIII went into voluntary exile rather than face a formal deposition. The Second Spanish Republic was proclaimed. When you were born that August, the republic was four months old and already under pressure from monarchists, the Catholic Church, the military, and various factions on the left. Within five years, it would be at war with itself. By 1939, Franco would rule. The Spanish Republic — born the same year you were, full of hope at the moment of your arrival — lasted eight years before it was extinguished.

**The Scottsboro case was convulsing the country.** In March 1931, nine Black teenagers, the youngest twelve years old, were pulled off a freight train in Alabama and charged with raping two white women. They were tried in rapid succession before all-white juries, convicted, and most sentenced to death, despite significant evidence against the accusations. By August 1931, the case had become an international cause — Communist organizations, civil rights groups, and foreign governments were demanding justice. The Supreme Court would eventually overturn the convictions twice. You were born into a country where this was the ongoing state of things: the law applied differently by race, openly, without apology, and the question of whether that would change was genuinely unresolved.

**The Depression had turned two years old, and nobody could see the bottom.** The Hoover administration continued to project confidence. Unemployment was around sixteen percent in August 1931 and climbing. Families were losing farms. Banks were closing in cascades. In Europe, the financial crisis that had started in America was spreading through banking systems across the continent. The generation around your parents had survived one world war and were watching their economic stability dissolve in what felt, at the time, like permanent collapse. The New Deal did not yet exist. The man who would build it — Franklin Roosevelt — was still Governor of New York.

---

**The arc of 95 years.**

You arrived on a date that had already seen a Roman city buried, an American capital burned, and a circumnavigation of the globe completed in a week. You were born into a Depression, survived a world war in your adolescence, and came out the other side into the long postwar boom that remade the industrialized world.

In your lifetime: the Spanish Republic you were born alongside was destroyed and eventually restored. The racial injustice visible in the Scottsboro case was legally dismantled — incompletely, slowly, against fierce resistance — over the decades of your adult life. The aviation that amazed the world with Post and Gatty's nine-day circumnavigation became so routine that most people gave it no more thought than taking a bus. The empire that burned Washington became America's closest ally. Pompeii is now a tourist destination.

Ninety-five years from a Monday in the Depression to now. The dates persist; the worlds around them change utterly.
